lesson.title: One Connection, Many Roads: How Multipath TCP Uses Every Link You Have
lesson.summary: Multipath TCP (MPTCP) extends ordinary TCP so a single connection can send data across several network paths at once, instead of being pinned to whichever interface it happened to start on.
lesson.body:
Regular TCP, as covered earlier, ties a connection to one path between two endpoints, identified by a fixed four tuple of source and destination IP addresses and ports. If a phone or laptop has both Wi-Fi and cellular radios active, a normal TCP connection still only uses whichever interface the socket happened to open on. If that link degrades or drops, the connection stalls or dies, even though a perfectly good second link may be sitting idle a few centimeters away inside the same device.

Multipath TCP fixes this by letting one logical connection span multiple physical paths. It is a real, standardized extension to TCP, originally published as RFC 6824 in 2013 and later revised into RFC 8684 in 2020, which moved it onto the IETF's full standards track. During the initial handshake, both endpoints negotiate MPTCP support using a TCP option. Once negotiated, either side can open additional subflows over different interfaces or paths, and MPTCP treats all of them as carrying pieces of one continuous byte stream. Each subflow behaves like an ordinary TCP connection underneath, with its own sequence numbers, acknowledgments, and congestion control, but MPTCP adds a data sequence number that sits above all the subflows, so the receiver can reassemble the original byte stream in the correct order no matter which subflow delivered which bytes.

The clearest real deployment of this idea is Apple's use of MPTCP for Siri traffic on iOS, in production since fairly early in iOS's history. A Siri request might start on a Wi-Fi subflow, and if that Wi-Fi link weakens, the device can already have a cellular subflow warmed up and ready, so the connection continues without a visible reconnect or a dropped request. This is a make-before-break style of resilience that single-path TCP simply cannot offer, because single-path TCP has no notion of a second path to fall back to.

MPTCP can also be used for throughput rather than just resilience, spreading a connection's data across multiple paths simultaneously to use their combined capacity, subject to congestion control that is deliberately coupled across subflows so that an MPTCP connection does not claim an unfair share of a bottleneck relative to ordinary single-path TCP flows crossing the same link. It is worth being precise about what MPTCP is not: it is not a QoS mechanism and does not prioritize any packets over others. It solves a path diversity and resilience problem. Prioritization, scheduling, and rate control on a given link are the job of the QoS mechanisms covered starting in the next chapter.
